title: QTc prolongation
summary: Which psychotropics prolong the QTc interval, who is at risk, when to do an ECG, and what to do at each QTc level.
keyPoints: Most QT-prolonging drugs block the cardiac **IKr (hERG) potassium channel**. The danger is **torsades de pointes**, which can cause syncope or sudden death [3].
**QTc >500 ms**, or a **rise of >60 ms** since starting the drug, needs action now: repeat the ECG, stop or switch the suspected drug, and refer to cardiology [1,2].

Highest effect: **pimozide, sertindole**, any **intravenous** antipsychotic, and doses above the maximum. **Citalopram, escitalopram**, several tricyclics and **methadone** have a moderate effect [1,2].
**Prevent it:** avoid combining QTc-prolonging drugs, use the lowest effective dose, and correct potassium, magnesium and calcium [1,2].
QTc is an **imperfect guide** to risk: the same QTc change carries different risk with different drugs and patients [1,3].

blocks.p: The QT interval runs from the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave: the total time for ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation [3]. Correct it for heart rate with the [QTc calculator](/qtc).

head: QTc
Meaning
rows: Substantially higher risk of torsades de pointes; act promptly [1,3]

blocks.p: A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia linked to prolonged repolarisation. On the ECG, the QRS complexes seem to twist around the isoelectric line [3].

facts.label: Symptoms
facts.text: Palpitations, dizziness, presyncope or syncope, cardiac arrest [3]

facts.label: Course
facts.text: May stop on its own, recur, or progress to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death [3]

facts.label: Not inevitable
facts.text: Risk also depends on the drug, electrolytes, heart disease and bradycardia [3]

head: Group
Risk factors
rows: Long QT syndrome, bradycardia, ischaemic heart disease, myocarditis, myocardial infarction, left ventricular hypertrophy [1]
Extreme physical exertion, stress or shock, anorexia nervosa, children and older people, female sex [1]
Other QTc-prolonging drugs, high doses, and drugs that raise the level of a QTc-prolonging drug [1,2]

blocks.note: Hypokalaemia-related QTc prolongation is more common in acute psychotic admissions. Genetic factors (cardiac potassium channels, CYP enzymes) may not show on routine examination but probably add risk [1].

sections.title: Drugs implicated
sections.sub: Antipsychotics [1]; antidepressants and other psychotropics [2]. Drugs not shown are not rated in these sources.

head: Effect
Meaning
rows: Large average QTc rise, usually **>20 ms** at normal doses [1,2]
Average rise **>10 ms** at normal doses, or ECG monitoring officially recommended in some situations [1,2]
Severe prolongation only in overdose, or small average rises **<10 ms** [1,2]
No prolongation reported at normal doses or in overdose [1,2]

blocks.note: Underlined drugs open their library page; grey names are not in the library. * Limited experience; an association may emerge [1]. † One case of TdP, two of QT prolongation and a database association with TdP; about **8 ms** QTc rise in healthy volunteers; low doses added to another antipsychotic have no effect [1]. ‡ Isolated cases; acts on the IKr channel; other data show no QTc effect [1]. § TdP common in overdose; strong association with TdP at clinical doses [1]. ¶ Inhibits P450, so may prolong QTc when combined with another QTc-prolonging drug [2].

Effect on QTc does not always equal risk of TdP or sudden death: ziprasidone has a moderate QTc effect but little evidence of cardiac toxicity. Ratings are approximate, and differences between antipsychotics rarely reach statistical significance [1].

head: Group
Drugs
rows: Erythromycin, clarithromycin, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, pentamidine; some quinolones [1]
Quinidine, disopyramide, procainamide, sotalol, amiodarone, bretylium [1]
Amantadine, ciclosporin, diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, methadone, nicardipine, tamoxifen [1]

blocks.note: Not a complete list. Beta-2 agonists and sympathomimetics may provoke TdP when QTc is already prolonged [1].

head: When
ECG
rows: Before an antipsychotic known to prolong QTc

Offer if the product information requires it, a cardiovascular risk factor is found (e.g. hypertension), there is a history of cardiovascular disease, or the patient is an inpatient or being admitted [2]
At steady state or the therapeutic dose

blocks.note: Check potassium, magnesium and calcium alongside the ECG [1,2].

items: Avoid QTc-prolonging drugs where possible, and avoid combining them: effects are likely additive [2].
Use the lowest effective dose and avoid drugs with significant metabolic interactions; QTc prolongation is likely dose-dependent [2].
Assess cardiac risk (personal and family history, symptoms, cardiovascular risk factors) before any moderate- or high-effect drug [2].
Discuss with cardiology first if there is cardiovascular disease, another significant risk factor, a current QTc-prolonging drug, or symptoms suggesting arrhythmia [2].
Look for drug and non-drug causes, and assess cardiovascular risk [2].
Bloods and ECG, with or without a 24-hour tape or echocardiogram [2].
Weigh the risk of continuing (QTc) against the risk of changing (relapse) [2].
Replace electrolytes; optimise cardiovascular risk and conditions such as thyroid disease or heart failure, usually with medical colleagues [2].

head: QTc
Action
Cardiology
rows: None, unless T-wave shape is abnormal [1]
Consider a lower dose or a lower-effect drug; repeat ECG [1]
>500 ms, or a rise of >60 ms since starting the drug
Repeat ECG; stop the suspected drug(s) and switch to a lower-effect drug [1,2]
Review treatment; consider a lower dose or a lower-effect drug [1]

blocks.callout: Also refer to cardiology if there are new unexplained cardiac symptoms with QTc >440 ms (men) or >470 ms (women), a history suggesting arrhythmia, a previous cardiac event, or the drug cannot be stopped or reduced [2].

blocks.p: Most drugs that cause acquired QT prolongation block the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current, **IKr**, carried by channels encoded by **KCNH2 (hERG)**. This is a cardiac ion-channel effect, not a synaptic one [3].

chains.title: From channel block to long QT
From long QT to torsades
steps: Early after-depolarisations (phase 2 or 3) cause premature beats: the trigger
Uneven repolarisation across the ventricles: the substrate
Trigger plus substrate: torsades de pointes

head: Phase
What happens
rows: Plateau: inward calcium balanced by outward potassium [3]

blocks.note: The QT broadly spans phases 0–3. Depolarisation happens in phase 0 only [3].

list: QTc prolongation is an imperfect surrogate for TdP [3].
The same QTc rise does not carry the same TdP risk across drugs or patients [3].
In congenital long QT, TdP risk rises by about **5–7%** (relative) for each extra **10 ms** of QTc [3]. This is not a validated risk calculator for psychotropics.
QTc ratings are mostly based on Bazett's correction, and QTc measurement is imprecise [1].
**hERG** is the old name for **KCNH2**, the gene for the IKr potassium channel [3].
Ventricular depolarisation is **phase 0** only; phases 1–2 are not depolarisation [3].
TdP: QRS complexes **twist around the isoelectric line**; it can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation [3].
**Ziprasidone**: moderate QTc effect but little evidence of cardiac toxicity [1].
**Paroxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline**: no QTc effect of their own, but P450 inhibition can raise levels of another QTc-prolonging drug [2].

drugRatings.name: Any drug or combination above the maximum dose

selfTest.question: A woman taking citalopram is started on haloperidol. A week later her ECG shows a QTc of 512 ms. She has no symptoms. What should you do?

options.text: Continue both and repeat the ECG in 6 months
Repeat the ECG, stop the suspected drug(s), switch to a lower-effect drug and refer to cardiology now
Reduce the citalopram dose and repeat the ECG in 1–2 weeks
Continue both; she has no symptoms

selfTest.explanation: A QTc above 500 ms needs a repeat ECG, stopping the suspected drug(s), a switch to a lower-effect drug and immediate cardiology referral [1,2]. Citalopram and haloperidol both have a moderate QTc effect, and combining QTc-prolonging drugs is likely additive [1,2].
